items.q: Which abiotic factor is used first to separate freshwater biomes from marine biomes?
options: Salinity
Water depth
Water color
Number of fish species

why.correct: Salinity, the amount of dissolved salt, separates freshwater (near 0) from seawater (about 35 parts per thousand).
options: Right: salt content is the main dividing line.
Both lakes and oceans have shallow and deep water.
Color is not a defining factor.
Fish numbers are biotic and depend on many things.

items.q: Why is an estuary such a rich place for young fish and shellfish?
options: Rivers bring nutrients, and the shallow, sheltered water gets plenty of sunlight.
Its water is colder and saltier than the open ocean.
It has no predators, so young animals are safe.
It is deep, so the water is dark and calm.

why.correct: Nutrients from rivers plus sunlit, shallow water let plants and algae grow fast, and marsh plants or mangroves shelter the young.
options: Right: nutrients plus light mean plenty of food, and the young find shelter.
Estuaries mix fresh and salt water, so they are less salty than the ocean.
Predators live in estuaries too; the young find shelter, not safety from every predator.
Estuaries are shallow, and light reaches the bottom.

items.q: Coral reefs grow in clear, warm, shallow water that is low in nutrients. Why does coral need clear, shallow water?
options: The algae living inside the coral need sunlight for photosynthesis.
Coral needs to be near the surface to breathe air.
Waves carry more food into shallow water.
Cold, deep water has too much oxygen for coral.

why.correct: Corals and the algae inside them are a mutualism: the algae make food from light and share it. Murky or deep water blocks the light.
options: Right: the coral’s partner algae need light.
Coral animals take oxygen from water; they do not breathe air.
Coral gets most of its food from its algae, not from waves.
Cold water holds more oxygen, but that is not why coral needs shallow water.

items.q: A biologist finds a coastal forest of salt-tolerant trees whose tangled roots hold mud in place, in a tropical area where a river meets the sea. What is it?
options: A coral reef
A mangrove forest
A temperate rainforest
An intertidal zone on a rocky shore

why.correct: Salt-tolerant trees with stilt roots along tropical coasts and estuaries are mangroves.
options: Coral reefs are underwater animal structures, not trees.
Right: salt-tolerant trees with tangled roots at a tropical river mouth.
Temperate rainforests are not salt-tolerant coastal trees.
A rocky intertidal shore has algae, barnacles and snails, not trees.

items.q: Organisms in the intertidal zone are covered by water at high tide and exposed to air at low tide. Which challenge do they face?
options: Drying out and being pounded by waves
Complete darkness for most of the day
Water that stays frozen solid through the year
Water with no dissolved oxygen

why.correct: The intertidal zone swings between wet and dry with each tide, and waves batter it, so its organisms resist drying and cling tightly.
options: Right: drying at low tide and wave force.
The intertidal zone is shallow and sunlit.
Temperatures vary but are not frozen year-round.
Moving, mixed water there is well oxygenated.

items.q: Wetlands such as marshes and swamps are often called "nature’s sponges." Which benefit does this describe?
options: They soak up floodwater and release it slowly.
They make the water around them saltier.
They raise the temperature of nearby rivers.
They remove sunlight from shallow water.

why.correct: Wetland soils and plants hold large amounts of water during floods and release it slowly, and they also filter pollutants.
options: Right: wetlands store floodwater and release it slowly.
Freshwater wetlands do not add salt.
Wetlands do not heat rivers.
Wetlands do not remove sunlight; their plants use it.

items.q: Which part of a lake is the shallow edge where rooted plants grow?
options: Littoral zone
Limnetic zone
Profundal zone
Benthic zone

why.correct: The littoral zone is the shallow, sunlit edge where plants can root in the bottom.
options: Right: the shallow edge with rooted plants.
The limnetic zone is open, sunlit water away from shore.
The profundal zone is deep water too dark for photosynthesis.
The benthic zone is the bottom sediment.

items.q: Why does each square meter of the open ocean grow so little algae, even though the ocean is huge?
options: Nutrients are scarce in the sunlit surface water.
The water is too salty for any algae.
There is too much light at the surface.
Seawater holds no dissolved oxygen.

why.correct: Algae need both light and nutrients. In much of the open ocean, nutrients sink below the sunlit surface, so algae grow slowly there.
options: Right: light is at the top, but nutrients are scarce there.
Marine algae thrive in salt water.
Light helps algae; too much light is not the limit.
Seawater does hold dissolved oxygen.

items.q: Explain why a warm, slow river can hold less oxygen for fish than a cold mountain stream.

why.correct: Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, and slow water mixes in less air.

specific.frame: As water temperature ___, the amount of dissolved oxygen the water can hold ___, so fish have ___ oxygen.

change.label: Temperature
options: increases
decreases

why.1: The river is warmer than the stream, so its temperature is higher.

direction.label: Oxygen held
options: decreases
increases

why.1: Warm water holds less gas than cold water.

effect.label: For fish
options: less
more

why.1: Less dissolved oxygen means less for fish to use.

specific.model: As water temperature increases, the amount of dissolved oxygen the water can hold decreases, which means fish in the warm river have less oxygen than fish in the cold stream.

items.q: Which site is an estuary, based on the data?
options: Site 1
Site 2
Site 3
Site 4

why.correct: An estuary mixes fresh and salt water, so its salinity is between 0 and about 35 ppt. Site 3 has 15 ppt.
options: Site 1 is fresh water (0 ppt).
Site 2 is fresh water (0 ppt).
Right: 15 ppt is in between fresh and ocean water.
Site 4 is full seawater (35 ppt).

items.q: Which relationship between temperature and dissolved oxygen do sites 1 and 2 show?
options: Warmer water had less dissolved oxygen.
Warmer water had more dissolved oxygen.
Temperature and dissolved oxygen were unrelated.
Salinity explains the difference in oxygen.

why.correct: Site 1 at 8 °C had 11.5 mg/L; site 2 at 24 °C had 6.0 mg/L. Both are fresh water, so salinity does not explain it.
options: Right: 24 °C with 6.0 mg/L vs 8 °C with 11.5 mg/L.
The warmer site had the lower value.
There is a clear difference that matches the temperatures.
Both sites have 0 ppt salinity.

items.q: How much more dissolved oxygen does the mountain stream (site 1) hold than the slow river (site 2)? Give the answer with its unit.

mistakes.why: You added the two values. "How much more" is a difference: 11.5 - 6.0.
You divided the two values. "How much more" asks for the difference: 11.5 - 6.0.

items.q: A student claims the open ocean (site 4) has low dissolved oxygen because it is salty. Do the data support the claim?
options: No: site 4 has more oxygen than the fresh, warm river at site 2.
Yes: site 4 has the lowest oxygen of the four sites.
Yes: oxygen falls steadily as salinity rises from site 1 to site 4.
No: site 4 has more oxygen than the cold mountain stream.

why.correct: Site 4 has 7.8 mg/L, more than site 2 (6.0 mg/L), so salt water here is not the lowest; temperature fits the pattern better.
options: Right: 7.8 mg/L at site 4 is above 6.0 mg/L at site 2.
Site 2 has the lowest value, 6.0 mg/L.
Oxygen does not fall steadily: site 2 (0 ppt) is lowest.
Site 4 (7.8) has less oxygen than site 1 (11.5).

items.q: About how much of the surface light is left at a depth of 4 m?
options: About 70%
About 30%
About 9%
About 55%
70% is the light lost by 4 m, not the light left.
Right: the curve passes 30% at 4 m.
9% is the value at 8 m.
55% is the value at 2 m.

items.q: Algae need at least about 1% of surface light to make more food by photosynthesis than they use. Where does the photic zone of this lake end?
options: At about 4 m
At about 8 m
At about 15 m
At the lake surface

why.correct: Light falls to 1.5% at 14 m and 0.8% at 16 m, so the 1% level is near 15 m. Below it is the aphotic zone.
options: At 4 m, 30% of the light is left, well above 1%.
At 8 m, 9% is left, still above 1%.
Right: between 14 m (1.5%) and 16 m (0.8%).
The surface has all of the light.

items.q: Rain after a storm washes mud into the lake and makes the water cloudy. How would the graph change?
options: Light would fall off faster, so the photic zone would be shallower.
Light would fall off more slowly, so the photic zone would be deeper.
The curve would not change, because mud does not block light.
The surface value would rise above 100%.

why.correct: Particles absorb and scatter light, so less reaches each depth. The 1% level moves up, and fewer algae and rooted plants can grow deep down.
options: Right: cloudy water blocks light, so the curve drops faster.
Mud blocks light; it does not let more through.
Suspended particles do block light.
The surface value is 100% by definition.

items.q: Which statement about salinity is correct?
options: Freshwater has very little salt; ocean water has about 35 parts per thousand.
Ocean water and freshwater have the same salinity.
Estuaries are saltier than the open ocean.
Lakes are saltier than estuaries.

why.correct: Freshwater is close to 0 ppt, seawater about 35 ppt, and estuaries are in between.
options: Right: near 0 ppt for freshwater, about 35 ppt for seawater.
Seawater is far saltier than freshwater.
Estuaries are diluted by river water, so they are less salty.
Most lakes are freshwater, less salty than estuaries.
